_note: Items with 'verify: true' had handwriting that was difficult to read precisely — confirm before publishing.
_note_no_fryer: There is no fryer. The kitchen is deli-style and nothing on this menu is deep-fried: the Fried Potatoes are pan-fried on the flat-top, the kids' tater tots and chicken strips come off the flat-top or out of the oven, and the chips come out of a bag. Do not add a deep-fried item without settling that first.
_note_serving: `serving` is an optional per-category time window ('Serving until 11am'). Breakfast stops at 11 and soup starts at 11 so the kitchen has time to change over; every menu template prints it next to the category name.
_note_price_review: Items with 'priceReview: true' are priced under $2.00 and are known to be stale — they date from the old menu and have not been re-costed yet. The tri-fold marks them with a red bullet ON SCREEN AND IN THE PNG EXPORT ONLY; the marker is hidden in print, so a proof shows the open questions but a real sheet never ships with them. Set the price and delete the flag.
_note_flat_price: A category whose items all cost the same carries ONE `sizing` line (wraps, kids meals) instead of repeating the number on every row — the same mechanism the salads use for Full/Half. Changing that price is then a one-line edit and there is no way for two rows to disagree. An item inside such a category may still carry its own `price`, which wins and prints on its row: that is how the two plates sit under the salads' Full/Half line. Trade-off, accepted: an item with no price of its own emits no schema.org Offer.
_note_picks: `picks` is a build-your-own category: a list of columns, each with a `label` and its `options`, printed side by side instead of as priced rows. It exists for the kids meals, where three mains x three sides as priced rows would be six rows all saying $6.00. A category with `picks` and no `items` is legal — every template guards the item list — and the JSON-LD flattens the options into MenuItems so the section is never published empty.
_note_hot_cold: Sandwiches are split into two categories, not one. 'Cold Sandwiches' is the deli case; 'Hot Sandwiches' is everything off the flat-top — the burgers AND the griddle sandwiches, merged into one category on 2026-09-29 at the client's call (they were 'Burgers or Chicken' plus a separate 'Hot Sandwiches'). The Clubhouse moved to the cold side at the same time. Every item names its DEFAULT bread — that default is what goes into Square as the item, and a bread swap is a modifier there — while the category note says the bread is a choice.
_note_build_sandwich: 'Build Your Own Sandwich' is its own category rather than rows inside Cold Sandwiches, so its prices never read as pricing the Clubhouse. The prices are ordinary priced rows (1 / 2 / 3 meats, half) rather than a `sizing` line: four pairs on one line wrapped mid-list on every layout and were hard to read down. The salads — curry chicken, walnut tuna and egg — sit in the SAME column as the meats because they count as one — the layout says it, so no sentence has to. Options are `picks`, like the kids meals. The curry chicken and walnut tuna salads are sold ONLY here: they were also separate Cold Sandwiches until 2026-09-30, removed because Build Your Own already covers them.
_note_default_bread: `defaultBread` is the bread a sandwich comes on when the customer does not ask — the item as it goes into Square, where any other bread is a $0 modifier. It is DATA ONLY and prints nowhere: the menus say 'with choice of bread' instead, and a bread line on every row would overrun the tri-fold. The rule, from the client 2026-09-30: WHITE unless the item names its own bread (Kaiser for burgers, rye for the Reuben and Patty Melt, hoagie for the Philly). Some sandwiches default to TOASTED white (Clubhouse, BLT) — that is part of the value, so 'White toast' and 'White' are different defaults. Toasting is a Square modifier either way.
_note_diet: Dietary marks are a data feature, not a nutrition claim. `diet` lists what an item IS as served; `dietOnRequest` lists what the kitchen can make it into if asked (drop the meat, hold the toast) and prints with an asterisk. Codes must exist in the `diets` registry below. The marks drafted here were read off the ingredient lists on this menu and have NOT been confirmed by the kitchen — `dietsConfirmed` is false, which puts a warning on the proof. Two deliberate omissions: drinks carry no marks (marking every bottle of water vegetarian is noise), and cured meats, bagged chips and bottled dressings are left unmarked because the gluten in those comes from a supplier label nobody has read yet. There is no low sodium mark: it was removed 2026-09-29 at the client's call (it was the LS code, mapped to schema.org LowSaltDiet) — do not reintroduce it without them. No wrap is called gluten free: the spinach wrap used to be named as the gluten free option, and that was withdrawn 2026-09-29 because nobody has confirmed which wrap (if any) actually is. Put it back only from the package label. Add marks only from a label or the kitchen, never from a guess. While `dietsConfirmed` is false the PUBLIC /menu page renders no marks at all — no key, no filter, no data attributes, no suitableForDiet — and says so in plain words instead. The tri-fold still shows them, because that is the proof the client reads in order to confirm them.
_note_diet_schema: `schema` is the schema.org RestrictedDiet the code maps to. /menu emits it as suitableForDiet on each item, which is how Google reads a dietary claim — so a code without one is invisible to search, and a WRONG one is a machine-readable false claim. Only `diet` items are emitted, never `dietOnRequest`: 'we can make it that way' is not something structured data can express, and publishing it as though it were would say the item ships gluten-free when it does not.
_note_health: The consumer advisory. This is the FDA Food Code's REMINDER — the general statement that undercooked animal foods carry a risk. It is triggered by eggs cooked to order (the omelets, the over-easy egg on a breakfast sandwich) and by burgers cooked to a customer's temperature, which is most of what this kitchen sells before 11am and a good deal of what it sells after. Seafood and shellfish are deliberately NOT in the wording: nothing on this menu is raw seafood, the tuna is canned, and listing foods a kitchen does not serve trains people to skip the line. Put them back the day a raw item goes on. The advisory has a SECOND half the Food Code calls the DISCLOSURE — marking WHICH items can be served raw or undercooked, usually with an asterisk on the item. That half is NOT implemented: it needs the kitchen to say which items they will cook to order, and a guessed asterisk is worse than none. Ask before adding it. Unlike the dietary marks, this is not gated behind dietsConfirmed and it is never proof-only. It prints, on every surface, always. It is the one line on this menu that exists for somebody who could get hurt.
healthNote: Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness, especially if you have certain medical conditions.
dietNote: Prepared in a shared kitchen. We are not a certified gluten-free facility and cannot promise against cross-contact. Please tell us about an allergy when you order.
